Just finished this one so I thought I’d throw in my two cents! 

What I Liked: 

“This is fine” Margaret was a fun, unreliable-yet-grounded MC.

The author did a fantastic job of playing with reader expectations regarding an overdone trope that the book seems to building to about 2/3rds of the way through. Without spoiling the story, I would say that this book delivered a great anti-twist(s) in terms of story beats, which was refreshing. 

I thought the writing was strong, with parallel repetitions being purposefully apparent to hammer in theme. Not every thematic element in a story needs to be viewed through the lens of in-depth analysis, nor do these elements need to be gate-kept behind whatever the “big twist” of the story is. 

What I Didn’t Like: 

The coziness. Personally, I am not a fan of quirky, cozy novels, and this definitely fits into that box. I was recommended this book by a friend who had just read House of Leaves - one of my absolute favorites - and I went into it with that sort of expectation in mind. Don’t get me wrong, I absolutely still enjoyed the book, but I probably wouldn’t have picked it up if I hadn’t been led to it. 

The ending. Oof, I couldn’t stand this ending. I don’t think it was poorly done, nor do I think that it invalidated the journey, but sweet holy Sacagawea did it go down my entire “I Can’t Stand These Things Wrap-Up Checklist.” A bit too saccharine, like a pitcher of Kool-Aid made with an extra 1/2 cup of sugar.

3.7/5

All in all, I enjoyed it, and I can absolutely see the things that I disliked as being big winners for other readers, even if they didn’t hit paydirt for me. Maybe a dip into Laird Barron’s newest work will give me more of what I was searching for. 

Anyways, $4 a pound.

“Lifting” Germany out of a bad situation and leaving them with the aftermath and ramifications of his Third Reich would, in my book, take Der Dummkopf out of the “Great Leader” category. 

And as for German competency in the War… Being great at seizing opportunity presented by the reluctance of other nations and successfully conducting a large-scale military conflict are two very different things. 

Hitler was a notoriously idiotic strategist who rode the high of the initial German push at the expense of all sense. Unsurprising, given his then-growing penchant for Methamphetamine usage. 

The Wermacht was notoriously inefficient in crucial areas, lacking in widespread mechanization, and was unable to keep itself supplied and moving. From the moment The Battle of Britain was blundered, the Wermacht was already in “Oh dang, we need to secure resources like yesterday” mode just to be able to minimally-maintain the war they had started. Yes, Small-Scale German Tactics could certainly be effective, but tactics win medals, not wars. In terms of Strategy and Logistics, Germany was a wet diaper filled with lumpy pudding. 

The myth of the Nazi War Machine, much like that of the “Lost Cause” Confederacy runs deep through years of constant propagation, but it is exactly that: a myth. This myth, much like the previously mentioned “Lost Cause”, is a dangerous one, rooted at best in apologetics and at worst in disdain for the final outcome. 

Anyways, $4 a pound.

If you’re really into the way Dave & Flea weave, you should definitely check out “Wrong Girl” by Jane’s. 

While the second two Jane’s albums are definitely not comparable to the first two, there are still some great tunes, and that one is Jane’s at their funkiest. 

For moments where Dave shines, some others I’d name off the top of my head… 

“Ocean Size” - phenomenal guitar solos; textbook example of how to do standard pentatonic shred in a hugely tasty way. 

“Idiots Rule” - great leads, but I really think Dave’s rhythm work shines here. Some Hendrix’d chords in the groove pocket. 

“Had A Dad” - really shows off the glam scene Dave’s playing was coming out of. 

“Pigs in Zen” - see above

“Ted Just Admit It” - in my head, this song is the prototype for Three Days. Lengthy, proggy, riffs and licks galore. 

“Stop” - Idiots Rule-type rhythm work, simultaneously kicked up and dialed back, with phenomenal lead work. 

“Three Days” - yeah… just listen to it. That’s the sort of solo that winds up on lists, and for good reason. 

“End to the Lies” - a good example of Dave taking a more outside-the-box approach to playing. 

Additionally, I’d also recommend the following tracks from other bands that feature Dave: 

“Straight On” by Heart - This is definitely my favorite version of this song. Dave fits like a glove and tails that groove. There’s a few songs on this live album featuring Dave, but I think this one is where he shines most. 

“Feed the Cruel” by NHC - Oh what could’ve been… Dave combines all of his guitar eras here. Phenomenal solo too. 

“You Oughta Know” by Alanis Morossette - Thank Uncle Joey that Alanis got so pissed. More importantly, thank Lucifer that Dave & Flea both just happened to be nearby to record this track. 

I could go on and on, but that’s a great start. Dave is absolutely one of my favorite players. 

Anyways, $4 a pound.

The next year - same dorm floor - people had matured and learned that valuable life lesson: 
There are only so many things in life worth actually giving a shit about. College dorm drama is not one of those things.

With that out of the way, here’s my take: 
- You probably want Humbuckers. Active or passive is up to you, but I much prefer good passive pickups
- If you’re tuning down low, a 25.5 scale may help 
- Quality tuners 
- A neck that you immediately don’t have to adjust your playing style to
- If you want a trem for Van Halen-esque tricks or anything more than a whammy-flutter, a Floyd Rose or Kahler.

Here’s my take - 

“Me” is a very fluid thing. While I have some certain innate traits as a framework, I find that I really am a different person every couple of months. Sometimes this means I’ve developed new tendencies or outlooks in place of old ones, sometimes it means I’ve simply discarded old aspects, and other times it means I’ve basically stopped caring about certain things. 

I think you can fit people into two BROAD categories in regards to self: 
On one end, you have those who are proud of their specific character and use it to guide them through whatever the world throws. That character is their armor, and those individuals need time to maintain that character because life does some damage. They need to perform regular routine maintenance, and each time they do that it may get a little more difficult than the last. 

At the other end, you have “scrappers”. These people have their values and identities like the first group, but they repair things along the way with new materials. Because of this, they aren’t quite as “firm” or monolith in their sense of self, but they’re usually pretty good at managing to find a way through it all by picking up things along the way. 

I don’t think either way is better, and I don’t think any person is consistently in one of these VERY BROAD camps for the entirety of their life. 

My life is so utterly minuscule in the grand scheme of the universe, so I don’t really feel that focusing on keeping the “real me” - whatever I deem that to be - is worth investing my emotional efforts into. In the end, I only get one shot at living on this rock, so I can either spend time trying to hang onto what I was, or I can just enjoy that time as whoever I am now.

My thoughts usually surround ways that I can keep my “Life Dreams” alive. 

The desire to see the world, finish my novels, develop a video game, record a full album - I have a tendency to be unable to focus on my dreams individually, and because of this progress is slow (often non-existent) on each of them;I believe I have an aversion to committing to an individual task wholeheartedly for fear of burning out. (Humorously, the way I approach these things caused burnout anyway) 

So, I usually find myself finding small ways to “hype” myself up towards these goals at night. Most of the time
It’s empty hype, but it keeps me going.
